details:
**The Canterbury Tales**
Chaucer's most famous work, a Middle English frame narrative from the late 1300s. A group of pilgrims riding to the shrine of Thomas Becket at Canterbury hold a storytelling contest, and each tells a tale. It is the most common title clue and the usual giveaway for Chaucer.

**The Wife of Bath's Tale: "what women most desire"**
In this Arthurian story, a knight who has raped a maiden is sentenced to death, but Queen Guinevere spares him on the condition that he find out what women most desire. An old hag gives him the answer, sovereignty or mastery over their husbands, in exchange for his hand in marriage. The Wife of Bath (Alisoun), a five-times-married woman, tells it.

**The Wife of Bath's Prologue**
In this long autobiographical prologue, the Wife recounts her marriages. She tore a page out of her fifth husband Jankyn's book of wicked wives, and he struck her on the ear so hard that she became "somewhat deaf."

**The Miller's Tale**
A bawdy tale told by the drunken Miller. The student "handy" Nicholas persuades the old carpenter John that a second Great Flood is coming, so John sleeps in a tub hung from the roof while Nicholas sleeps with his young wife Alisoun. The suitor Absolon is tricked into kissing Alisoun's "nether eye" (her backside). When Nicholas later farts in his face, Absolon brands him with a hot iron (coulter).

**The Knight's Tale: Palamon, Arcite, and Emily**
The first of the Canterbury Tales, adapted from Boccaccio's Teseida. The imprisoned Theban cousins Palamon and Arcite both fall in love with Emily (Emelye), Theseus's sister-in-law. Arcite wins the tournament for her but is crushed when his horse falls, so Palamon marries her. The story later inspired Shakespeare and Fletcher's The Two Noble Kinsmen.

**The Tabard Inn and the General Prologue**
The Canterbury Tales opens with a General Prologue that begins with "April's sweet showers" ("Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote"). It describes the "sundry folk," about 29 pilgrims, who gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark. The Host, Harry Bailly, proposes the storytelling contest.

**Troilus and Criseyde**
Chaucer's long poem about two lovers during the Trojan War, adapted from Boccaccio's Il Filostrato and written in rhyme royal. Criseyde, daughter of the seer Calchas, is exchanged as a prisoner to the Greeks. She breaks her promise to return to Troy in ten days and takes Diomede as her lover. It is often cited as the source of the phrase "all good things must come to an end."

**The House of Fame**
A dream poem in which the narrator, a version of Chaucer, wakes in a glass temple of Venus and sees the story of the Aeneid (Dido and Aeneas) engraved on a brass tablet. A golden eagle carries him to the House of Fame and then to a spinning wicker house. It contains the first recorded English use of the word "galaxy."

**The Parlement of Foules**
A dream vision in which Scipio Africanus leads the narrator to a garden where birds gather before the goddess Nature on St. Valentine's Day to choose mates. Three eagles court a female eagle while lower birds such as the duck mock courtly love. It is one of the earliest texts to link Valentine's Day with romance.

**The Pardoner's Tale**
A moral tale in which three rioters set out to kill Death. An old man directs them to an oak tree, where they find a pile of gold coins, and they then murder one another over it, so all three find Death after all.

**Sir Thopas**
Chaucer includes himself as a pilgrim, and his tale "Sir Thopas" is a parody of a chivalric romance in which the knight dreams of an Elf Queen and meets a giant. The Host interrupts it, saying his "dirty rhyming is not worth a turd." Chaucer then tells the prose Tale of Melibee.

**The Book of the Duchess**
Chaucer's early dream poem, an elegy for Blanche of Lancaster, first wife of John of Gaunt. It opens with Ovid's story of Ceyx and Alcyone. A knight in black then tells the dreamer how he lost his "queen" in a game of chess against Fortune.

**The Prioress and her Tale**
The Prioress, Madame Eglantine, swears only "by Saint Loy" and wears a brooch reading "Amor vincit omnia." Her tale tells of a young Christian boy whose throat is cut by Jews but who keeps miraculously singing the hymn "Alma Redemptoris Mater" until a grain is removed from his tongue.

**Other Canterbury tales and pilgrims**
In the Friar's Tale, a summoner tries to extort a frying pan from a poor widow, who curses him to the devil. In the Summoner's Tale, a friar is challenged to divide a fart into twelve equal shares, solved with a cartwheel. In the Squire's Tale, the king Cambuskan receives a flying brass horse and his daughter Canacee gets a ring that lets her speak with a falcon. In the Franklin's Tale, Dorigen promises herself to the squire Aurelius if he can remove the rocks from the coast. The Parson ends the collection with a sermon on the seven deadly sins.

**Treatise on the Astrolabe and the short poems**
Chaucer's prose manual on using the astrolabe, written for his young son Lewis. His short poems include "The Complaint of Chaucer to His Purse," the triple roundel "Merciless Beauty," and "Anelida and Arcite." He translated Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy and was the first poet buried in Westminster Abbey's Poets' Corner.
